rv.q: If this is a test of her ability to lead a tricky Shakespeare play and imbue it with verve and coherence, she's passed.
This production is, within its concept, generally a joy.
This labour of love doesn’t always pay off, then.
Lown-Collins’ production doesn’t really do much to combat these issues – the Latin is simply swapped for Spanish quips, and the ending is still the ending.
It works; but more clarity wouldn’t go amiss.
Stylish, sexy but strangely lacklustre, this shallow take on Shakespeare’s seldom-produced comedy feels overly laboured despite a vibrant design and the evident energy of its cast.
The result, however, is a crude cacophony of impenetrable Spanish accents, punctuated by groin thrusts and clumsy pratfalls, with nothing to say about love, learning or loss.
This is a blazing, joyful triumph.
Lown-Collins doesn’t attempt to bypass any of these issues, instead redirecting our attention to the production’s bold new flamenco theme.
What could have been a gimmick proves irresistible, with an abundance of creativity, energy, and heart.
This creative approach is the best of both worlds.
The choreography, colour, and high spirits have the crowd fully on side.
This version of Love’s Labour’s Lost is certainly the craziest production at the Globe for a long time.
This production is a triumph in each aspect and proves that reinvigorating Shakespeare’s works is entirely possible, and should even be encouraged if it leads to more performances like this one.

Overall, Love’s Labour’s Lost at Shakespeare’s Globe is a vibrant summer production that successfully combines one of Shakespeare’s most challenging comedies with the passion and expressiveness of flamenco.
Caveats aside, this joyously silly production is perfect for a warm summer’s evening.
This is a fantastic reimagining of Shakespeare’s comedy, a magnificent celebration of the English language and its witty quirks, and a showcase for the ferocious power of flamenco.

cn.t: This flamenco-infused production brings vibrant Spanish flair and energy to Shakespeare's tricky early comedy, with most critics praising its creativity and joyful spectacle, though some feel the flashy concept overshadows the Bard's intricate wordplay.
